lessons.title: Say hello
lessons.subtitle: Greetings for every time of day

theory.title: Greetings follow the clock
theory.body:
Serbian greetings change through the day: dobro jutro in the morning, dobar dan during the day and dobro veče in the evening. Laku noć is only for bedtime or leaving late at night.

Zdravo and ćao are informal — use them with friends. Ćao means both hi and bye.

Notice dobro / dobar: "good" changes its ending to match the word after it. Jutro and veče are neuter (dobro), dan is masculine (dobar). You will see this pattern everywhere.

challenges.explanation: Dobro jutro, Kristina! — Good morning, Kristina!
You heard: Ćao, vidimo se! — Bye, see you!
Dobro veče, Ana! — Good evening, Ana!
You heard: Laku noć i hvala! — Good night and thank you!
Zdravo, Marko! — Hello, Marko!
You heard: Doviđenja i hvala! — Goodbye and thanks!
Dobro jutro, Ana! — Good morning, Ana!
Dobar dan! — Good day!
Laku noć! — Good night!
“Dobro jutro!” — “Dobro jutro! Kako si?”
“Ćao, vidimo se sutra!” — “Ćao, vidimo se!”

lessons.title: Be polite
lessons.subtitle: Please, thanks and the two kinds of "you"

theory.title: Ti or Vi?
theory.body:
Serbian has two words for "you". Use ti with friends, family and children. Use Vi with strangers, older people, shop staff and anyone in a formal situation. Vi is also the plural "you".

Many polite words come in both forms:
• izvini / izvinite — sorry, excuse me
• hvala ti / hvala vam — thank you

Molim is a multi-tool: "please", "you're welcome" and "pardon?" when you didn't catch something.

challenges.explanation: Izvinite, molim vas. — Excuse me, please.
You heard: Ne, hvala. — No, thanks.
Da, hvala vam. — Yes, thank you.
You heard: Hvala ti, Ana! — Thank you, Ana!
Izvini, Marko! — Sorry, Marko!
Izvinite, molim vas. — Excuse me, please.
Hvala ti, Jelena! — Thank you, Jelena! (to a friend)
Nema problema. — No problem.
“Hvala vam!” — “Molim.”
“Izvini!” — “Nema problema.”

lessons.title: How are you?
lessons.subtitle: Ask and answer, friendly or formal

theory.title: Kako si? Kako ste?
theory.body:
Kako si? asks a friend how they are. Kako ste? is the polite form, and also the plural.

Answer with Dobro sam — sam means "I am". Throw the question back with A ti? or A Vi?

Some words show who is speaking: a man says umoran sam, a woman says umorna sam. The extra ‑a for women is one of the most common patterns in Serbian.

challenges.explanation: Kako si, Ana? — How are you, Ana?

challenges.answer: I am fine thanks And you
challenges.explanation: You heard: Dobro sam, hvala. A ti? — I am fine, thanks. And you?
Odlično, hvala! — Great, thanks!
You heard: Kako ste danas? — How are you today?
Umorna sam danas. — I am tired today.
Dobro sam, hvala. — I am fine, thanks.
Kako ste, gospodine? — How are you, sir?
Ja sam Ana i umorna sam. — I am Ana and I am tired.
challenges.translation: I am Ana and I am tired.
challenges.audioText: Ja sam Ana i umorna sam.

challenges.explanation: “Kako si?” — “Dobro sam, hvala. A ti?”
“Kako ste?” — “Odlično, hvala. A Vi?”

challenges.explanation: Kristina: Hi, Miloš! How are you? Miloš: Not bad, but I am tired. And you? Kristina: Great!

theory.title: One letter, one sound
theory.body:
Serbian is written in two alphabets, Cyrillic (ћирилица) and Latin (latinica). Both are official and every Serb reads both.

Each letter always has the same sound, so once you know the letters you can read any word aloud.

Special Latin letters: č and ć (both close to "ch"), š (sh), ž (the s in "pleasure"), đ and dž (close to "j"), lj and nj (as in "million" and "canyon"), and j, which always sounds like "y".

Cyrillic look-alikes that sound different: В = v, Н = n, Р = r, С = s, Х = h.

units.title: Who I am
units.subtitle: Names, the verb "to be", countries and jobs
outcomes: Use sam, si, je, smo, ste, su
Say where you are from and where you live

theory.title: Zovem se…
theory.body:
Zovem se literally means "I call myself". The se stays and the verb changes: zovem se (I), zoveš se (you), zove se (he / she).

Ask: Kako se zoveš? (friend) or Kako se zovete? (polite).

When you meet someone, say Drago mi je — "nice to meet you". The usual answer is I meni (me too).

Introduce others with Ovo je…: Ovo je Ana, moja prijateljica.

challenges.explanation: Zovem se Ana. — My name is Ana.
You heard: Kako se zoveš? — What is your name?
Ovo je Marko, moj prijatelj. — This is Marko, my friend.
You heard: Drago mi je, Jelena. — Nice to meet you, Jelena.
Ona se zove Kristina. — Her name is Kristina.
Kako se zoveš? — What is your name?
Zovem se Miloš. — My name is Miloš.
Ovo je Ana, moja prijateljica. — This is Ana, my friend.
“Kako se zoveš?” — “Zovem se Nikola.”

challenges.audioText: Zdravo! Zovem se Jelena. Ovo je Marko, moj prijatelj.

theory.title: Biti — to be
theory.body:
ja sam · ti si · on / ona / ono je
mi smo · vi ste · oni su

The ending already tells you who, so the pronoun is often dropped: Student sam = Ja sam student.

These little forms never start a sentence: say Ja sam… or Student sam…, not Sam student.

Serbian has no "a" or "the": Ja sam student = I am a student.

You heard: Ona je studentkinja. — She is a student.
Mi smo ovde. — We are here.
You heard: Oni su prijatelji. — They are friends.
Gde si ti? — Where are you?
You heard: Vi ste Kristina? — Are you Kristina?
Mi smo studenti. — We are students.
Ona je ovde. — She is here.
Ja sam Ana. Ja sam studentkinja. — I am Ana. I am a student.

theory.title: Iz and u
theory.body:
Iz means "from" and changes the country's ending: Srbija → iz Srbije, Engleska → iz Engleske, Amerika → iz Amerike (‑a becomes ‑e).

U means "in" and uses another ending: u Srbiji, u Engleskoj, u Londonu, u Beogradu.

For now, learn them as fixed phrases. The pattern will click with practice.

You heard: Odakle si ti? — Where are you from?
Živim u Beogradu. — I live in Belgrade.
You heard: Ana je iz Srbije. — Ana is from Serbia.
Marko živi u Londonu. — Marko lives in London.
You heard: Mi smo iz Amerike. — We are from America.
Ja sam iz Srbije. — I am from Serbia.
Živim u Beogradu. — I live in Belgrade.
Odakle si? — Where are you from?
“Odakle si?” — “Ja sam iz Australije.”

lessons.title: What do you do?
lessons.subtitle: Jobs for him and for her

theory.title: Jobs come in pairs
theory.body:
The masculine form usually ends in a consonant. The feminine form adds an ending:
• nastavnik → nastavnica
• lekar → lekarka
• konobar → konobarica
• student → studentkinja

To ask what someone does, say Šta radiš? Answer with Ja sam lekar. There is no word for "a".

challenges.explanation: Ja sam nastavnica. — I am a teacher.
You heard: On je lekar. — He is a doctor.
Šta radiš? — What do you do?

units.title: Things around me
units.subtitle: Noun gender, adjectives, colours and places
outcomes: Tell masculine, feminine and neuter nouns apart

theory.title: Every noun has a gender
theory.body:
You can almost always tell a noun's gender from its ending:
• masculine — a consonant: sto, telefon, ključ
• feminine — ‑a: knjiga, torba, olovka
• neuter — ‑o or ‑e: pismo, ogledalo, more

Gender matters because the words around a noun change to match it: moj telefon, moja knjiga, moje pismo.

challenges.explanation: Šta je ovo? — What is this?
You heard: Ovo je moj telefon. — This is my phone.
Ovo je moja knjiga. — This is my book.
You heard: Ovo je moje pismo. — This is my letter.
Gde je moja torba? — Where is my bag?

challenges.answer: The key is on the table
challenges.explanation: You heard: Ključ je na stolu. — The key is on the table.
Ovo je moj telefon. — This is my phone.
Ovo je moja olovka. — This is my pen.
Ovo je moje ogledalo. — This is my mirror.
“Šta je ovo?” — “Ovo je knjiga.”

theory.title: Adjectives copy the noun
theory.body:
An adjective takes the gender of its noun:
• masculine — no ending: nov telefon
• feminine — ‑a: nova knjiga
• neuter — ‑o: novo pismo

That is why it is dobar dan but dobro jutro! Dobar loses its second a when it adds an ending: dobra, dobro.

Veliki and mali usually keep their ‑i in the masculine: veliki grad, mali stan.

challenges.explanation: Beograd je veliki grad. — Belgrade is a big city.
You heard: Ovo je nova knjiga. — This is a new book.
Telefon je skup. — The phone is expensive.
You heard: Moja torba je mala. — My bag is small.

Knjiga je jeftina. — The book is cheap.
“Telefon je skup?” — “Ne, jeftin je.”
“Kakva je kafa?” — “Odlična je!”

challenges.question: What is new?
challenges.explanation: My town is small but beautiful. My house is old, and my phone is new. The book is cheap.
challenges.audioText: Moj grad je mali, ali lep. Moja kuća je stara, a moj telefon je nov. Knjiga je jeftina.

theory.title: Colours agree too
theory.body:
Colours are adjectives, so they change like nov:
• crven telefon, crvena torba, crveno pismo
• plav, plava, plavo — blue

Beo (white) is a little special: beo telefon, bela kuća, belo pismo.

Ask about colour with Kakve je boje…? — "of what colour is…?"

challenges.explanation: Moja torba je crvena. — My bag is red.
You heard: More je plavo. — The sea is blue.
Sunce je žuto. — The sun is yellow.
You heard: Kakve je boje knjiga? — What colour is the book?
Knjiga je zelena. — The book is green.
You heard: Moj telefon je siv. — My phone is grey.
Olovka je žuta. — The pen is yellow.
Pismo je belo. — The letter is white.
Sto je crn. — The table is black.
“Kakve je boje tvoja torba?” — “Crvena je.”
“Da li je more zeleno?” — “Ne, more je plavo.”

challenges.question: What colour is the book?
challenges.explanation: My room is small and white. The table is white, the pen is yellow, and the book is black.
challenges.audioText: Moja soba je mala i bela. Sto je beo, olovka je žuta, a knjiga je crna.

theory.title: Gde je…?
theory.body:
Gde je…? asks where something is. Answer with ovde (here), tamo (there), blizu (near) or daleko (far).

To say "on" and "in", use na and u. The noun changes its ending:
• sto → na stolu (on the table)
• torba → u torbi (in the bag)
• kuća → u kući (in the house)

Pored (next to) and ispod (under) work the same way: pored telefona, ispod stola. Learn them as phrases for now.

units.title: Everyday verbs
units.subtitle: Have, not, questions and languages
outcomes: Talk about the languages you speak

theory.title: Imati — to have
theory.body:
imam · imaš · ima · imamo · imate · imaju

Imati is a regular ‑am verb. Learn it and you know hundreds of verbs that work the same way.

After "have" (and most verbs), feminine nouns change ‑a to ‑u: Imam sestru, Imam mačku.

Masculine things stay the same (Imam auto, Imam telefon), but people and animals add ‑a: brat → Imam brata, pas → Imam psa.

challenges.prompt: I have a brother and a sister.
challenges.explanation: Imam brata i sestru. — I have a brother and a sister.
You heard: Imaš li psa? — Do you have a dog?
Ana ima mačku. — Ana has a cat.
You heard: Mi imamo auto. — We have a car.
Imam novi telefon. — I have a new phone.
Imam sestru. — I have a sister.
Marko ima psa. — Marko has a dog.
Imamo mačku. — We have a cat.
“Imaš li brata?” — “Da, imam brata.”
“Imate li auto?” — “Da, imamo auto.”

theory.title: Ne, nisam, nemam
theory.body:
Put ne before a verb to make it negative: ne znam, ne razumem, ne radim.

Two verbs fuse with ne into one word:
• biti → nisam, nisi, nije, nismo, niste, nisu
• imati → nemam, nemaš, nema…

Nema also means "there isn't": Nema problema!

Serbian loves double negatives: Nikad ne pijem kafu (I never drink coffee). The ne stays even with nikad or ništa.

lessons.title: Asking questions
lessons.subtitle: Da li, who, where, when, why

theory.title: Questions
theory.body:
Turn any statement into a yes/no question with Da li at the front: Imaš psa → Da li imaš psa?

Or put li straight after the verb: Imaš li psa? Both are correct.

Question words go first: Šta radiš? Ko je to? Gde živiš? Kada radiš? Zašto učiš srpski?

Answer zašto (why) with zato što (because).

theory.title: Three verb families
theory.body:
Serbian verbs fall into three families by their "I" form:
• ‑am: imam, znam
• ‑em: razumem
• ‑im: govorim, radim

The "you" form swaps ‑m for ‑š: znaš, razumeš, govoriš. For he / she, drop the ‑m: zna, razume, govori.

Life-saving phrases: Govorite li engleski? · Ponovite, molim vas. · Sporije, molim vas.

theory.title: Numbers that agree
theory.body:
Jedan (one) is an adjective and agrees with its noun: jedan sto, jedna kafa, jedno pismo.

Dva (two) has a feminine form: dva telefona, but dve kafe.

After numbers, the noun ending changes: dve kafe, pet kafa. Don't worry about the rules yet. Learn the phrases and listen for the pattern.

Age uses imati: Imam dvadeset godina — "I have twenty years".

Tri i četiri je sedam. — Three and four is seven.
Ovo je jedna olovka. — This is one pen.

theory.title: Bigger numbers
theory.body:
11–19 add ‑naest: jedanaest, dvanaest, trinaest…
Tens add ‑deset: dvadeset, trideset, četrdeset, pedeset.

Combine them freely: dvadeset pet (25), sto dvadeset (120).

Sto means both "hundred" and "table". The context decides!

Prices use the dinar: jedan dinar, dva dinara, pet dinara.

theory.title: Ordering: ‑a becomes ‑u
theory.body:
When you order, the thing you want is the object, so feminine words change ‑a to ‑u:
• kafa → Jednu kafu, molim.
• voda → Vodu, molim.

Masculine and neuter drinks don't change: čaj, sok, pivo, vino.

Želim (I would like) is polite. Finish with Račun, molim! and don't forget hvala.

theory.title: The present tense
theory.body:
Almost every verb ends in ‑m in the "I" form:
• ‑am: gledam, spavam, ručam
• ‑im: radim, učim
• ‑em: ustajem, idem

Change ‑m to ‑š for "you": radiš, gledaš, ideš. Drop the ‑m for he / she: radi, gleda, ide.

Time words: ujutru (in the morning), posle podne (in the afternoon), uveče (in the evening).

theory.title: Jesti and piti
theory.body:
Two very common verbs are irregular:
• jesti (eat): jedem, jedeš, jede, jedemo, jedete, jedu
• piti (drink): pijem, piješ, pije, pijemo, pijete, piju

Meals: doručak, ručak, večera. In Serbia ručak is the big meal, often eaten around two or three o'clock.

Hungry: gladan sam (man) / gladna sam (woman).

theory.title: Telling the time
theory.body:
Koliko je sati? — literally "how many hours is it?"

The word for hour changes after the number:
• jedan sat (1)
• dva, tri, četiri sata (2–4)
• pet sati and up (5–12)

Half past is i po: sedam i po = 7:30. "At" a time is u: u osam, u podne.

Timetables use the 24-hour clock.

theory.title: On Monday…
theory.body:
Days are not capitalised in Serbian.

"On Monday" is u + the day. The feminine days change ‑a to ‑u:
• u ponedeljak, u utorak, u četvrtak, u petak
• but u sredu, u subotu, u nedelju

Nedelja also means "week". Danas (today), sutra (tomorrow), juče (yesterday).

theory.title: In and at: the locative
theory.body:
Where are you? U parku, u školi, u gradu.
• masculine and neuter add ‑u: park → u parku, centar → u centru
• feminine ‑a becomes ‑i: škola → u školi, bolnica → u bolnici

Some places take na instead of u: na trgu, na pijaci, na pošti, na stanici. Learn which one goes with each word.

theory.title: Polite commands
theory.body:
Directions use the polite command form, which ends in ‑ite:
• idite — go
• skrenite — turn
• pitajte — ask

Idite pravo — go straight. Skrenite levo — turn left. Na semaforu — at the traffic lights.

Start with Izvinite, gde je…? (Excuse me, where is…?)

theory.title: How you travel
theory.body:
Serbian needs no word for "by". The noun takes a new ending, ‑om or ‑em:
• autobus → autobusom
• voz → vozom
• tramvaj → tramvajem
• taksi → taksijem

On foot is peške. By car is usually kolima.

Ask Kada polazi voz? (When does the train leave?) and Sa kog perona? (From which platform?)

On the boards: polazak = departure, dolazak = arrival, kasni = delayed.

theory.title: Moj, moja, moje, moji
theory.body:
"My" agrees with the noun it describes:
• moj otac, moj brat — masculine
• moja majka, moja sestra — feminine
• moje dete — neuter
• moji roditelji — plural

Mama and tata are the everyday words for mum and dad. Žena means both "woman" and "wife".

theory.body:
Possessives behave like adjectives: tvoj brat, tvoja sestra, tvoje ime.

Njegov (his) and njen (her) depend on the owner. Their ending matches the thing owned:
• njegova majka — his mother
• njen otac — her father

Vaš is also the polite "your": Kako je Vaše ime?

theory.body:

• feminine ‑a → ‑i: u kuhinji, u sobi

• kuća → u kući

theory.title: A disappearing a
theory.body:
Some adjectives drop an a when they add an ending:
• ljubazan → ljubazna
• pametan → pametna
• zabavan → zabavna
• nizak → niska (the z becomes s, too)

Describe hair and eyes with imati: Ona ima dugu kosu i plave oči. Kosa becomes kosu, the ‑u for objects again.

theory.title: Volim vs sviđa mi se
theory.body:
Volim takes an object, so feminine ‑a becomes ‑u: volim muziku, volim kafu, volim fudbal.

Sviđa mi se works the other way round. The thing is the subject and stays unchanged: Sviđa mi se muzika means "music is pleasing to me".

For plural things it's Sviđaju mi se filmovi.

theory.title: Hobby verbs
theory.body:
Šta radiš u slobodno vreme? — What do you do in your free time?

Most hobby verbs are regular:
• ‑am: igram, slušam, čitam, plivam
• ‑im: trčim
• ‑ujem: putujem. Verbs in ‑ovati become ‑ujem: putovati → putujem, kupovati → kupujem.

Say how often: često (often), ponekad (sometimes), nikad ne (never).

theory.title: Inviting and answering
theory.body:
Invite with Hoćeš li…? (do you want to…?) or simply Idemo na kafu? (shall we go for coffee?).

Say yes with Može! (sure) or Važi! (deal). Say no kindly: Žao mi je, ne mogu.

Going somewhere uses u / na plus the ‑u ending: idemo u bioskop, na žurku, na kafu.

Polite and plural forms add ‑te: pišite, zovite.

Messages are short: Kasnim 5 minuta! Stižem! Čujemo se!

theory.title: The future
theory.body:
The future uses ću, ćeš, će, ćemo, ćete, će plus the verb.

When the verb comes first and ends in ‑ti, the ‑ti drops and the two fuse:
• raditi → radiću
• videti → videćemo
• biti → biću

Verbs in ‑ći keep a space: ići ću, doći ću.

With a pronoun or another word first: Ja ću raditi. Sutra ću raditi.

challenges.explanation: Sutra ću raditi. — Tomorrow I will work.

Marko će biti ovde. — Marko will be here.

theory.title: Modal verb + da
theory.body:
Modal verbs take da plus a present-tense verb. This is the Serbian way of saying "to":
• Moram da radim — I must work
• Mogu da dođem — I can come
• Hoću da spavam — I want to sleep

Both verbs change for the person: Moraš da učiš.

Treba mi pomoć — "help is needed to me" — means I need help.

theory.title: Going there vs being there
theory.body:
Going to a place uses u / na plus the ‑u ending. Being there uses the locative:
• Idemo na planinu → Na planini smo.
• Idemo na more → Na moru smo.
• Idemo u selo → U selu smo.

theory.title: Checking in
theory.body:
At reception: Imam rezervaciju na ime… (I have a reservation under the name…).

Imate li slobodnu sobu? (Do you have a free room?)

Za dve noći (for two nights): noć becomes noći after two, three and four.

You will need your pasoš at check-in.

theory.title: Was, worked, went
theory.body:
The past tense is sam / si / je… plus a past form that shows the speaker's gender:
• radio — a man
• radila — a woman
• radili — a group

So Kristina says Bila sam u Beogradu and Miloš says Bio sam u Beogradu.

Ići (to go) is irregular: išao / išla.

Word order: Ja sam radio, or without the pronoun, Radio sam.

theory.title: We were…
theory.body:
The plural past uses smo / ste / su plus ‑li: bili smo, išli smo, jeli smo, pili smo.

To say how something was, use bilo je plus an ‑o word: Bilo je lepo! Bilo je zabavno. Bilo je dosadno.

This neuter ‑o form is how Serbian describes situations in general.

theory.title: It is warm
theory.body:
Weather sentences have no "it": Toplo je (it's warm), Hladno je, Sunčano je, Oblačno je. That's the ‑o form again.

Rain and snow "fall": Pada kiša, Pada sneg. Duva vetar means the wind blows.

Vreme means both "weather" and "time".

Seasons: proleće, leto, jesen, zima. "In summer" is leti, "in winter" is zimi.
